title: Visual Basic tutorial: VB.NET syntax, types, collections and classes — cv.cm
description: Learn Visual Basic .NET: create a project, declare variables with Dim, use If, Select Case and loops, functions, List, Dictionary, classes, LINQ and Try.
answer: Visual Basic .NET (VB.NET) is an object-oriented, statically typed language for the .NET platform with English-like keywords such as `Dim`, `If ... Then ... End If` and `For ... Next`. It is not case-sensitive and uses the same .NET libraries as C#. Create a project with `dotnet new console -lang VB` and run it with `dotnet run`. VBA, the macro language inside Microsoft Office, is an older relative with similar syntax.

sections.h: What Visual Basic .NET is and who uses it
body: VB.NET is the .NET successor of classic Visual Basic (VB6). It compiles to the same intermediate language as C#, so the two languages can share libraries and even be mixed in one solution. It is used mainly for Windows desktop applications (Windows Forms, WPF), internal business tools, ASP.NET web applications and the maintenance of existing VB code bases.

Microsoft continues to support Visual Basic on modern .NET, but it has said that it does not plan to evolve the language with major new features; new .NET features usually appear in C# first. For a new project without existing VB code, C# is the more common choice, but VB.NET remains a readable language for learning programming and for business software.
Install the .NET SDK (Windows, macOS or Linux). Visual Studio on Windows also includes Visual Basic templates and a visual form designer.

body.code:
dotnet new console -lang VB -o HelloVB
cd HelloVB
dotnet run
# Hello, world!

' Program.vb
Imports System

Module Program
    Sub Main(args As String())
        Console.WriteLine("Hello, world!")
    End Sub
End Module

body: A `Module` holds shared procedures, and `Sub Main` is the entry point. Comments start with an apostrophe `'`. Each statement normally ends at the end of the line; there are no semicolons or braces.

Declare variables with `Dim name As Type`. With `Option Infer On` (the default) you can omit the type when you assign a value. Put `Option Strict On` at the top of each file (or set it in the project) so that risky implicit conversions become compile errors.

body.code:
Option Strict On
Module Types
    Sub Main()
        Dim name As String = "Ana"
        Dim age = 30                  ' inferred as Integer
        Console.WriteLine(name & " is " & age.ToString())
        Console.WriteLine($"Next year {name} is {age + 1}")
        Console.WriteLine(7 / 2)      ' 3.5 (always Double)
        Console.WriteLine(7 \ 2)      ' 3 (integer division)
        Console.WriteLine(7 Mod 2)    ' 1
    End Sub
End Module

Dim score = 85
If score >= 90 Then
    Console.WriteLine("A")
ElseIf score >= 80 Then
    Console.WriteLine("B")
Else
    Console.WriteLine("C")
End If

Select Case score
    Case 90 To 100
        Console.WriteLine("excellent")
    Case 80 To 89
        Console.WriteLine("good")
    Case Else
        Console.WriteLine("keep going")
End Select

For i = 1 To 3
    Console.WriteLine($"{i} squared is {i * i}")
Next

Dim n = 3
Do While n > 0
    n -= 1
Loop

body: These statements go inside a `Sub`. `For i = 1 To 3` includes both ends; add `Step -1` to count down. `For Each item In collection` loops over any collection. Use `Exit For` or `Exit Do` to leave a loop early. For conditions, prefer `AndAlso` and `OrElse`: they stop evaluating as soon as the result is known, while `And` and `Or` always evaluate both sides.

A `Sub` does not return a value; a `Function` does. Parameters are passed `ByVal` (a copy) by default; `ByRef` lets the procedure change the caller's variable. Parameters can be `Optional` with a default value.

body.code:
Function Add(a As Integer, b As Integer) As Integer
    Return a + b
End Function

Sub Greet(Optional name As String = "world")
    Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {name}!")
End Sub

Sub Increment(ByRef value As Integer)
    value += 1
End Sub

' Inside Sub Main:
Dim x = 5
Increment(x)                                  ' x is now 6
Greet()                                       ' Hello, world!
Dim square = Function(n As Integer) n * n     ' lambda
Console.WriteLine(square(Add(1, 2)))          ' 9

Dim nums() As Integer = {3, 1, 2}
Dim five(4) As Integer            ' 5 elements, indexes 0 to 4
Array.Sort(nums)
Console.WriteLine(String.Join(", ", nums))   ' 1, 2, 3

Dim names As New List(Of String) From {"Ana", "Ben"}
names.Add("Cleo")
Console.WriteLine(names.Count)               ' 3

Dim ages As New Dictionary(Of String, Integer)
ages("Ana") = 30
ages("Ben") = 17
For Each pair In ages
    Console.WriteLine($"{pair.Key}: {pair.Value}")
Next

body: Arrays and lists are indexed from 0 with parentheses: `nums(0)`. Generic types use `Of`: `List(Of String)` is the VB form of C#'s `List<string>`. Note that `Dim five(4)` declares the upper bound, not the length, so the array has five elements.

sections.h: Signature features: classes, properties and LINQ queries
body: VB.NET is fully object-oriented: classes have properties, methods, constructors (`Sub New`), inheritance (`Inherits`), interfaces (`Implements`) and events (`Event`, `RaiseEvent`, `Handles`). LINQ queries can be written in a readable query syntax.

body.code:
Public Class Person
    Public Property Name As String
    Public Property Age As Integer

    Public Sub New(name As String, age As Integer)
        Me.Name = name
        Me.Age = age
    End Sub
End Class

' Inside Sub Main:
Dim people As New List(Of Person) From {
    New Person("Ana", 30),
    New Person("Ben", 17)
}
Dim adults = From p In people
             Where p.Age >= 18
             Select p.Name
For Each adultName In adults
    Console.WriteLine(adultName)   ' Ana
Next

body: Because VB is not case-sensitive, `Name` and `name` are the same identifier; inside the constructor, `Me.Name` refers to the property and `name` to the parameter. Other VB-specific conveniences include `With ... End With` blocks, XML literals and the `My` namespace for common tasks.

VB.NET uses structured exception handling: `Try`, `Catch`, `Finally` and `Throw`. A `Catch` can include a `When` filter. The older `On Error GoTo` style from VB6 and VBA still compiles but should not be used in new .NET code.

body.code:
Function ParseAge(s As String) As Integer
    Dim n As Integer
    If Not Integer.TryParse(s, n) Then
        Throw New FormatException($"Not a number: {s}")
    End If
    If n < 0 Then Throw New ArgumentOutOfRangeException(NameOf(s))
    Return n
End Function

' Inside Sub Main:
Try
    Console.WriteLine(ParseAge("abc"))
Catch ex As FormatException
    Console.WriteLine("Error: " & ex.Message)   ' Error: Not a number: abc
Finally
    Console.WriteLine("done")
End Try

sections.h: A small complete program: word frequencies

body.code:
Imports System
Imports System.Collections.Generic
Imports System.Linq

Module WordCount
    Sub Main()
        Dim text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"
        Dim counts As New Dictionary(Of String, Integer)

        For Each word In text.Split(" "c)
            If counts.ContainsKey(word) Then
                counts(word) += 1
            Else
                counts(word) = 1
            End If
        Next

        Dim top = counts.OrderByDescending(Function(kv) kv.Value).Take(2)
        For Each kv In top
            Console.WriteLine($"{kv.Key} {kv.Value}")
        Next
    End Sub
End Module
' the 3
' and 2

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: thinking `Dim a(4)` creates four elements (it creates five); using `And`/`Or` where a short-circuit `AndAlso`/`OrElse` is needed, for example `If x IsNot Nothing And x.Length > 0` fails when `x` is `Nothing`; expecting `/` to do integer division (use `\`); leaving `Option Strict Off`, which hides type errors until run time; and confusing VB.NET with VBA, whose code and libraries are different.

sections.h: VBA: Visual Basic inside Microsoft Office
body: Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) is the macro language built into Microsoft Office applications such as Excel, Word and Access. It is based on classic Visual Basic, not .NET: it runs inside the Office application, uses the Office object model (workbooks, ranges, documents), and is edited in the VBA editor (Alt+F11 on Windows). The basic syntax of `Dim`, `If`, `For` and `Sub` is the same, which makes VB.NET knowledge useful for VBA.

body.code:
' VBA in Excel: write the squares of 1 to 5 into column A
Sub FillSquares()
    Dim i As Long
    For i = 1 To 5
        Cells(i, 1).Value = i * i
    Next i
    MsgBox "Done"
End Sub

ul: Microsoft Learn: the Visual Basic documentation, including the getting-started guide and the language reference.
Learn the .NET base class library (collections, files, LINQ); it is shared with C#.
For desktop apps, try Windows Forms or WPF templates in Visual Studio.
For Office automation, read the VBA reference on Microsoft Learn for the application you use.

faq.a: No. It is supported on current .NET versions and in Visual Studio, but Microsoft does not plan major new language features, so most new .NET projects choose C#.

faq.q: What is the difference between VB.NET and VBA?
faq.a: VB.NET is a full .NET language for building standalone applications. VBA is a macro language based on classic Visual Basic that runs inside Office applications such as Excel; the syntax is similar, but the runtime and libraries are different.

faq.q: Should I learn VB.NET or C#?
faq.a: If you maintain VB code or want very readable syntax, VB.NET is fine. For new projects, job opportunities and the newest .NET features, C# is usually the better investment, and the libraries you learn transfer between the two.
No. `Dim Total`, `total` and `TOTAL` all refer to the same variable, and the editor usually normalizes the capitalization for you.
